# Reference: Product Category & Deployment Model

What each of the six offerings actually IS — the form factor a buyer installs and runs. See [`citations.md`](../citations.md) for sources.

## What "the offering you install" means per platform

**Claude Code** is the most surface-diverse: a CLI is the canonical interface, but Anthropic ships first-party support for VS Code, JetBrains (beta), a standalone Desktop app on macOS/Windows including ARM64, a web UI at `claude.ai/code`, an iOS app, plus integrations for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Slack, and Chrome [2]. Each surface "connects to the same underlying Claude Code engine, so your CLAUDE.md files, settings, and MCP servers work across all of them" [2].

**Cursor** is the pure fork-IDE play: the user downloads `cursor.exe` (or .dmg/.AppImage), and Cursor IS the editor — there is no Cursor extension for VS Code or JetBrains [7]. The product evolved from "smart editor" toward "agent orchestrator" with Cursor 2.0 (2025) introducing Composer agent mode and Cursor 3 (~April 2026) adding the Agents Window for parallel multi-repo execution.

**GitHub Copilot** has the broadest IDE coverage in the market: VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains family, Neovim, Eclipse (2024-03+), Xcode (8.0+), Azure Data Studio [15]. It also has a CLI, a web-based "Copilot Workspace" planning environment, and a cloud-hosted "Copilot Coding Agent" that opens PRs from issue assignments. The April 20, 2026 signup pause affects only Pro, Pro+, and Student tiers — Free, Business, and Enterprise can still register new users [12].

**Gemini coding products are three distinct things** — this is the framing problem most direct prompts elide. **Gemini Code Assist** is an IDE plugin distributed via marketplaces for VS Code, JetBrains, Android Studio, Cloud Workstations, and Cloud Shell Editor [17]. **Gemini CLI** is a separate open-source (Apache 2.0) terminal agent. **Antigravity** is a third, distinct surface: a standalone VS Code fork (not a plugin), launched in public preview Nov 20, 2025 with a "Manager Surface" for orchestrating multiple parallel agents [18].

**Windsurf** is both an IDE fork (Windsurf, formerly Codeium) and a multi-IDE plugin set. The IDE itself ships the Cascade agent and (Max+) Devin Cloud sessions; the plugins for VS Code/JetBrains/Vim/Neovim/Xcode bring more-limited Cascade functionality to other editors [21][24]. The marketplace listing for the VS Code extension still uses the legacy ID `Codeium.codeium` even though the brand has migrated.

**IBM Bob** is two products under one name: **Bob-IDE**, "a full fork of VS Code, which gives IBM complete control over the environment and avoids the limitations that come with maintaining a complex extension on top of another editor" [27]; and **Bob Shell**, a separate terminal CLI installable via a curl one-liner. Bob-IDE imports VS Code settings and extensions on first run, plus preferences from Cursor and Windsurf [27]. The IT Jungle GA article describes Bob as a "VS Code plug-in" [26], but the December first-look [27] is explicit that it is a fork; the December source is more authoritative on architecture.

## What changed between research start and finish

This dimension is the single most-volatile in the comparison. Within the **last 11 days** of the April 26, 2026 research date:
- April 15, 2026: Windsurf 2.0 + Devin-in-Windsurf launched [22][39]
- April 20, 2026: GitHub paused Copilot Pro/Pro+/Student signups [12][13]
- April 22, 2026: Anthropic silently moved Claude Code to Max-only on the pricing page, then reverted within hours [5]
- April 24, 2026: GitHub Copilot interaction-data policy effective for Free/Pro/Pro+ [14]

A buyer reading this in May 2026 should re-verify each of those.

## Gaps and limitations

- IBM Bob's exact GA architecture (fork vs plug-in) has conflicting characterizations across IT Jungle's own coverage [26][27]; this analysis trusts the December first-look [27] over the March GA-day characterization [26], since the former describes the product directly while the latter writes "VS Code plug-in" as shorthand.
- The IBM Project Bob official announcement page (`ibm.com/new/announcements/ibm-project-bob`) returned HTTP 403 to in-session fetches; product positioning data comes from IT Jungle, the Register, and developer blogs.
- Cursor 3's release date and feature scope come from third-party coverage (InfoQ) rather than Cursor's own changelog read in-session.
- Gemini Antigravity's GA timeline (still public preview as of April 2026) is documented but no fixed GA date has been published.
